sentences.text: The type species of the genus is named Samrukia nessovi. The species name honors paleontologist Lev Nessov, while the genus name refers to Samruk, a magical bird from Kazakh folklore.
Samrukia is known only from a single lower jaw fossil found in Kazakhstan.
If Samrukia could fly, it might have had a wingspan of nearly 4 meters and weighed 12 kg; if it could not fly, it would have been 2 to 3 meters tall and weighed over 50 kg.
Samrukia was described by Darren Naish, Gareth Dyke, Andrea Cau, François Escuillié, and Pascal Godefroit in 2012.
The only known specimen of Samrukia was collected from the Santonian-Campanian age Bostobynskaya Formation in the Kyzylorda District.
Researchers initially interpreted Samrukia as a very large bird with a jawbone twice as long as that of an ostrich.
Researchers interpreted Samrukia as a large bird with a mandible twice as long as that of an ostrich.
Samrukia lived during the Santonian to Campanian stages, from 85.7 to 72.2 million years ago.
Eric Buffetaut challenged the interpretation of Samrukia as a bird in a 2011 analysis.
Buffetaut argued that characteristics previously identified as avian were actually well known among pterosaurs.
Buffetaut criticized the original analysis for excluding pterosaurs, noting that the analysis only included birds and other theropod dinosaurs.
Buffetaut concluded that the species was clearly a large pterosaur rather than a giant bird.
Darren Naish, one of the original researchers, agreed with Buffetaut's reassessment that Samrukia was a pterosaur.
Darren Naish admitted that working with fragmentary material was dangerous and realized shortly after publication that Samrukia was a pterosaur, not a bird.
A review by Averianov et al. suggested Samrukia was an Azhdarchid pterosaur and possibly a synonym of Aralazhdarcho.
